scenario.brief: Your company is running an internal hackathon: build a rough concept for reducing customer support response time, in 45 minutes, working solo. You have time for planning, not full execution.
scenario.context: The skill being tested isn't coding speed — it's picking one genuinely solvable slice of a big problem instead of trying to solve everything.

steps.title: Scoping the Challenge
steps.prompt: Given only 45 minutes, what's the strongest scoping approach?
options: Try to design a complete AI-powered support system covering every ticket type
Pick one narrow, specific sub-problem (e.g., auto-routing the 3 most common ticket types to the right team) and design that well
Spend most of the time researching what competitors do before starting
Focus entirely on the visual design of a dashboard, without addressing the actual response-time problem
steps.reasoning: Picking one narrow, well-defined sub-problem and designing it well is what actually produces something concrete and presentable in 45 minutes — attempting a comprehensive system guarantees a shallow, unfinished result across everything rather than a genuinely thought-through solution to one real piece of the problem.
steps.tip: In any time-constrained ideation exercise, deliberately narrow your scope in the first few minutes before starting to design — the biggest risk to a good 45-minute output is trying to cover too much ground.
steps.mistake: Attempting to design a comprehensive solution covering 'every ticket type' in 45 minutes almost always produces a shallow, generic result that doesn't actually demonstrate real problem-solving on any specific piece.
steps.recommendation: Time-box your scoping decision itself — spend the first 5 minutes deciding exactly what narrow slice you'll solve, then commit to it rather than second-guessing the scope partway through.

steps.title: Your Concept Pitch
steps.prompt: Write a 3-4 sentence pitch for your scoped concept (auto-routing the 3 most common ticket types).
steps.modelAnswer: My concept: auto-route the three most common support ticket types (password resets, billing questions, and shipping status) directly to specialized queues based on simple keyword detection in the ticket subject line, bypassing the general triage queue entirely. These three categories currently represent roughly 40% of all tickets based on typical support volume patterns, so even this narrow slice could meaningfully reduce overall response time without needing complex AI. I'd validate this by testing keyword accuracy against a sample of last month's actual tickets before building anything, to make sure the auto-routing doesn't misroute a meaningful number of tickets.
steps.reasoning: A strong hackathon pitch names the specific, narrow scope clearly, explains why this particular slice matters (the volume percentage), and includes a validation step before claiming success — this shows disciplined, realistic thinking rather than an overconfident, unvalidated idea.
steps.tip: Include a specific validation step in your pitch (testing against real historical data) — it shows you're thinking about whether the idea would actually work, not just presenting an untested assumption as a solution.
steps.mistake: A pitch that describes an idea without any sense of its actual expected impact (like the 40% volume figure) is much less convincing than one that connects the narrow scope back to real, quantified value.
steps.recommendation: Practice compressing your pitch to under 60 seconds spoken — a hackathon pitch that runs long, even with a good idea, often loses the audience before getting to the point.

outcome.reflectionPrompt: If you had a real 45 minutes to prototype a solution to a problem you care about, what narrow slice would you choose to tackle first?
